I have some posts on Reddit that went more than 2 parts and it was a big pain keeping track of the word counts and I found it hard to keep a solid train of thought forcing me to go back and reread things several times to make sure I had covered all the bases.

Of course discussion may inevitably involve someone posting an entire novel. I don't think there's a problem with that at all.

Some day everyone across the globe will all have a true Gb connection where we no longer have to be concerned with these things. But until then, be patient and structure your verbose comments accordingly.

I always saw it on Reddit, but never really read enough to understand it. Well, that and Reddit has a tendency of deleting stuff they don't like. What is Kotaku, GamerGate, and as someone who plays video games frequently, why should I care about this?

In a nutshell:

GamerGate is a scandal involving unethical conduct amongst video game journalists (including, amongst other things, failing to disclose relationships they have with developers/publishers and failing to label certain forms of paid advertising content as such in order to distinguish it from independently-written content).

Kotaku is one of several websites whose employees are involved in the scandal; other notable examples include Gamasutra, Polygon, Rock Paper Shotgun, and Destructoid.

A few resources to get you started:

  • GamerGate in 60 Seconds
  • If It's Not About Ethics...
  • Chris von Csefalvay's four-part analysis of the GamerGate Twitter network (which debunks the oft-reported claim that GamerGate is about harassment and discrimination); One, Two, Three, Four
  • GamerGate Press Dossier
  • Know Your Meme: GamerGate

To take your questions slightly out of order:

First, Zoe Quinn is largely irrelevant these days. Indeed, she was only tangentially relevant to begin with, and then only because of the apparent conflicts of interest due to relationships she had with certain game reviewers (reviewers who allegedly provided favorable coverage for her game Depression Quest in exchange for favors).

As for why Quinn is largely irrelevant these days, it's because this incident was revealed to be one in a long line of incidents of unethical conduct (e.g. Doritosgate, the Shadow of Mordor Incident, and the blacklisting of Allistair Pinsof to name just a few); many of these incidents were revealed due to a leak from a private email group called GameJournoPros.

To use an analogy I came across elsewhere, if we were to focus solely on Quinn's antics to the exclusion of the rest of the unethical conduct we'd unearthed, it'd be like focusing on the actions of Gavrilo Princip while the First World War is raging around us.

Now, as for GamerGaters, those are the people who have been critical of the unethical practices revealed by the GameJournoPros leak and who want the various outlets involved to adopt codes of ethics like those outlined by the Society of Professional Journalists and the Reuters Handbook of Journalism.

Which brings me to the last of your questions.

I assume you're talking about the phrase "actually, it's about ethics in journalism"? Yeah, it's intended as an insult - mainly by social-justice extremist types who like to use it as a 'gotcha!' in a discussion (while conveniently forgetting that 'gotcha!'s don't work the way they think they do).

GamerGate activist: "These particular outlets employ these people, who have been involved in these incidents of unethical conduct. [$EVIDENCE] Something has to be done about this!"

GG activist: "What the hell does [$irrelevant incident] have to do with anything?"

SJE: "Oh, you're talking about [$irrelevant incident] now? I thought GamerGate was about ethics in video game journalism, why are you talking about [$irrelevant incident]?"

What is Kotaku

It's a video games news/journalism site.

GamerGate

People got ticked off at how much it seems almost all games journalists (At Kotaku, Polygon, etc) give no shits about basic journalistic ethics. A commonly used source for ethical practices that all journalists should follow is here. There are a ton of violations of that code in a lot of the articles these journalists write, one of the most commonly noted ones being that journalists write about people they personally know and refuse to disclose it.

Why should I care?

Journalists have power and, as such, have the responsibility to use it in ways that generally don't suck. Sounds cliche, but it's true. You shouldn't have a situation where being quoted by EA's head of Digital Communications in a public blog leads to a journalist doing the equivalent of crying to that person's parents, leading to the whole blog being marked private. If you want to see what the blog post was, here's an archived version.

Many journalists have taken a stance of "If I don't like it/ it disagrees with my politics, it shouldn't exist", which is very, very dangerous. If they can silence someone in a high-up position of a massive company for just quoting them, imagine what they could do to indie developers that they dislike. In that case, it wouldn't be just one person's blog, but potentially a whole team's livelihood down the drain over a disagreement. IIRC, it's very hard to make it as an indie developer and even harder to live off of it, which is why that could be a death-blow to their indie dev career.

Think of your favorite indie game. Imagine it not existing at all because some journalist decided to ruin their will to create. They have the power to do that, and they've shown that they're willing to try to use it.

But turn it around. What if those journalists decide to promote a game made by a close friend? What if they decide to use their power to ensure their friends become the poster children of "The Indie Gamedev Scene", regardless of the quality of their work? What if those journalists use their power to push an agenda on their readers?

Again, these journalists have been abusing their power. Sometimes, it's harmless (like clickbait), but we're seeing them use it in harmful ways. You'll often hear from those against #Gamergate how pro-#Gamergate people are basically straight white cisgender neckbearded misogynists who harass women because they can't handle the idea of a woman being equal to men or some bullcrap, and that's a lie a lot of these journalists ran with. Now, any time any person decides to criticize one of these journalists, they're immediately labeled as "part of the #GamerGate hate group" and dismissed as not being worth listening to. Every legitimate concern from people who these journalists have interacted with before are being swept under the rug, save for a few sites.

TL;DR: Journos (Like those at Kotaku) are abusing their power, which could lead to games you'd like never being made. GamerGate is basically a hashtag a lot of people who are pissed at that prospect use to share info and ideas.
